newsitem.title: JAPAN: Kao speeds move into Asian household products mart.
newsitem.headline: Kao speeds move into Asian household products mart.

text.p: A mature domestic market has forced Japanese household products giant Kao Corp to accelerate the pace of its expansion into Asia, but it faces stiff competition from global rivals.
"It's a necessary move. Household products have reached saturation point in the domestic market, and the only way to boost profit is to conquer new markets," an industry analyst said.

Kunio Shimizu, director of public relations at Kao, said the company aims to increase sales in Asia by 20 percent every year from the current 60 billion yen ($545 million) to 70 billion yen ($636 million).

Kao made its first move into other Asian markets about 30 years ago, but it has bolstered its activities in recent years with the establishment of a fully owned subsidiary in Vietnam last December and the completion in China earlier this month of a plant to make sanitary pads.
Kao also makes chemical products in Taiwan and the Philippines, and is building a plant in Shanghai.
Chemicals used as ingredients for products including shampoo and concrete are exported worldwide, and Kao is already a big player in this sector in Asia.
But Kao also expects to compete head on with Unilever and Procter & Gamble Co (P&G), two other major producers of household goods, in the personal care products sector in Asia.
Back home, Kao holds the largest share of the shampoo market at 19 percent followed by P&G's 14 percent. In household detergents it has a 27 percent share against P&G's 25 percent.
Unilever and P&G are at the moment the two biggest players in Asia, and Kao is struggling to catch up, analysts said.

"Kao is a well-known brand in the region, but the two other companies are more popular, and their distribution channels are well-established," said Kumi Miyauchi, an analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research Ltd.

"We're confident in the competitiveness of our products, but we need to raise investment in marketing, R&D, and the education of employees. Kao is a small firm compared to Unilever and P&G, but we are aiming for even competition," said Kao's Shimizu.
Some analysts say Kao's strength in research and development places it in a good position to capture the Asian market. "Kao has the ability to develop unique, innovative products," said Miyauchi.
But others say Kao needs to focus more on the needs of Asian consumers, which may differ from country to country.

Keiko Sasaki, an analyst at Barings Securities Ltd, said Kao has to keep in mind that the Asian market is still in its infancy, and at times the company's standards are too high in terms of price and quality for consumers in the region.
"P&G and Unilever's products are of high quality in Japan, but not necessarily in Asia," she said.
Kao needs to seek a balance between high-quality, high-priced products and basic, economical products like its foreign counterparts, she said. ($1=110 yen)
